one_liner: Parallel Rust disk-usage CLI with a dust-style tree chart; 2.7-10x faster than dust, mixed against pdu.
what_it_does: zdu is a `du` replacement that walks a tree in parallel and prints dust's tree chart with percent bars. It began as a port of dust v1.2.5 and keeps dust's CLI shape (-d depth, -n count, -s apparent size, -f file count, -x one filesystem, -L follow links, regex/type/size/time filters, -j JSON, --files-from). It is a command-line tool only; there is no library API.
how_it_is_fast: The walk runs as flat rayon scope tasks (no recursion): each directory is read once into a Vec, entries are processed with into_par_iter clamped to a 64-entry minimum leaf, and each subdirectory spawns its own task that bubbles its node up via an atomic pending counter. Hard-link dedup uses a 256-shard Mutex<HashSet<(inode, device)>> sharded on the inode, which the source says cut /nix/store from 818 ms to 631 ms versus a device-keyed shard; directories are classified from readdir d_type instead of an extra stat. On Windows, DirEntry::metadata() reuses the FindNextFile data so plain entries need no per-file stat.
when_to_use: Interactive disk-usage inspection where you want dust's tree chart but faster on large trees (hundreds of thousands to millions of files).
Link-heavy trees such as /nix/store, where the README shows 402.7 ms vs pdu -H 1.401 s and dust 1.118 s.
Windows/NTFS scans: README shows 2.7-7.4x over dust and 2.0-6.2x over pdu on 7.6k-163k file trees.
Many-core machines with warm page cache, the only setting measured (32 logical cores).
when_not_to_use: Small trees on Linux: pdu -H beat it on ~/.cargo (14.0 ms vs 19.6 ms).
When you need a library to embed in a C++ program; this is a Rust binary.
Cold-cache or spinning-disk scans: not benchmarked; diskus and gdu siblings publish cold-cache numbers.

When you need exact GNU du semantics: allocated size is capped heuristically (blocks*512 replaced by size rounded to blksize when it exceeds that by more than 65536 blocks), and Windows counts plain-file hard links once per link.
Production use requiring maturity: 0 stars, first commits and release all in September 2026.

integration.dependencies: rayon, clap, regex, serde/serde_json, chrono, lscolors, nu-ansi-term, terminal_size, config-file, ctrlc, stfu8, thousands, unicode-width; on Windows filesize and winapi-util
integration.platforms: Linux/Unix and Windows (both benchmarked); macOS not documented
integration.thread_safety: not applicable (CLI); internally multithreaded via rayon
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — CLI flags largely follow dust (it is a dust port), but not pdu's flags or output format; installed crate name is zdu-rs, binary zdu

gotchas: The README links pdu to XAMPPRocky/pdu, but the versions benchmarked (0.21.1, 0.24.0) and the -H/--deduplicate-hardlinks flag match KSXGitHub/parallel-disk-usage.
No benchmark script is published; the tables give hyperfine means only, with no CPU model or variance.
Every regular entry's (inode, device) goes into the dedup set in default mode, not only entries with link count above 1, so memory grows with file count; -s (apparent size) skips dedup.
zdu renders a full tree while pdu prints a flat list, so the comparison is not output-equivalent (README argues this favors pdu).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick zdu over pdu (parallel-disk-usage) when you want dust's tree output, are on Windows, or scan link-heavy trees; pick pdu for small Linux trees and diskus when you only need a single total, since diskus publishes cold-cache numbers and zdu does not.
verified_claims_summary: Author's hyperfine runs with warm page cache on 32 logical cores (CPU not named): on Linux, zdu 19.6/143.8/402.7 ms vs dust 1.2.4 at 202.2 ms/388.2 ms/1.118 s and pdu 0.21.1 -H at 14.0/228.3/1401 ms for 57k, 509k and 1.2M files; on Windows 10/NTFS 2.7-7.4x over dust 1.2.3 and 2.0-6.2x over pdu 0.24.0 without -H. Release build uses LTO and codegen-units=1; no other flags or harness published.
status_note: Active (88 commits, last 2026-09-18) but brand-new with 0 stars; MIT OR Apache-2.0, installable with cargo install, usable as a CLI tool rather than copyable library code.
